description: We're ORBITRONS, a team of four B.Sc. IT students united by our love for space and games. We're beginners in technology, but not in thinking. Driven by curiosity, we're learning, experimenting and turning ideas into reality with the resources we have. Through Orbit Quest, we aim to make space exploration exciting and accessible while helping players appreciate the science and scientists behind every mission. For us, every great discovery starts with curiosity.
summary:
# Lunar Rescue

Lunar Rescue is a two-dimensional space-flight and survival game for desktop. An astronaut is stranded on the Moon, their oxygen is running out, and you are the only one who can reach them in time.

Before launch, you design your mission on a budget of one thousand million dollars. Choose a lifter, an engine, and a trajectory, then spend what remains on propellant, life support, shielding, and landing systems. Every choice affects your fuel, oxygen, and hull strength.

Then fly the lander across 384,400 kilometres to the Moon. Land upright and gently beside the beacon, take the astronaut aboard, and return to base. Collect fuel cells, dodge meteors, escape high-gravity zones, and survive solar storms in later sectors. Four difficulty levels, from forgiving Cadet to brutal Legend, suit every pilot.

Build your profile with a name and avatar, earn experience, and climb six ranks from Cadet to Mission Chief. Spend coins in the Hangar on upgrades like a magnet and hull plating. Choose from four visual themes, including retro Apollo 1969 and Neon Synthwave, or switch to a first-person cockpit view.

The game is self-contained, works offline, and runs on Windows as a desktop app. Progress saves automatically.

That is exactly 200 words, counting the title. I can also write a 50-word or 100-word version.
details:
Here are the benefits of playing Lunar Rescue, based on how the game works.

For the player

Planning and decision-making. Before each flight you split a $1000M budget between the rocket, the engine, the trajectory, and the on-board systems. Because more fuel means less shielding, you learn to weigh trade-offs and accept that no single design is perfect.

Hand-eye coordination and control. Landing upright at under 10 m/s means managing thrust, rotation, and speed together. With practice, your reaction time and precision improve.

Resource management. Fuel, hull, and astronaut oxygen all run down at once. The game trains you to prioritise under pressure.

Basic space and physics concepts. The game touches on engine efficiency, payload limits, transfer routes, gravity, and landing speed. It's a light, playful introduction, though not a simulator.

Calm problem-solving under stress. Meteors, high-gravity zones, and solar storms push you to stay composed and adapt.

Steady progress and motivation. XP, six ranks, coins, and Hangar upgrades make every run count, even a failed one.

Replayability. Four difficulty levels, four visual themes, and two camera views give you reasons to keep coming back. Beating your best score adds a personal goal.

Short, flexible sessions. A rescue is quick enough for a break, and progress saves automatically.

For you as the creator

  • Works offline. There is no server, no sign-in, and nothing to maintain.
  • Small and self-contained. A single file of about 500 KB is easy to share and update.
  • Wide reach. It runs in a browser or as a Windows desktop app, and it supports touch controls.
  • Good for a portfolio. It shows planning systems, a profile system, progression, themes, and generated audio in one project.
  • Ready to publish. It suits itch.io, a website, or a Steam-style store page.

These benefits are general. The game is entertainment first, so the learning is a bonus.

If you want, I can turn this into a "Key Features" section for a store page, or write a version aimed at parents or teachers.
